newsitem.title: UK: Hanson Energy seen parting post-flotation.
newsitem.headline: Hanson Energy seen parting post-flotation.

text.p: The mighty Hanson's Energy Group will be the last of its four units to be demerged early 1997, but analysts see little strategic fit and some are already predicting a possible divorce of the Peabody Coal and Eastern electricity partnership.

The Energy group comprises Peabody Coal, the largest U.S. coal producer with a 14 percent market share and a place in the worldwide top ten and Eastern, Britain's biggest electricity distributor which has become one of its main generators as well as one of the top three independent gas suppliers.
UBS energy analyst Iain Turner dubbed the pair "The Odd Couple" of the Hanson demerged empire. "Their combination creates no additional value," he said.
Energy Group is one of four companies to be split under the demerger together with Millennium Chemicals and Imperial Tobacco on October 1, leaving the stand-alone rump Hanson building firm.
The Energy group is estimated to be floated for around 2.5 billion pounds ($3.92 billion). It has sales of 3.52 billion and profits of 461 million and debt will be around 1.4 billion pounds.
But despite the apparent synergy within Energy Group, analysts say it creates little value and point to the future logic of splitting the two.
"As Eastern and Peabody walk down the aisle together the question asked is will they remain together. I don't think so," said Nigel Hawkins, utilities analyst at Yamaichi International.
Yamaichi's Hawkins explained there was little commercial logic in Eastern using Peabody's mainly U.S.- based coal supplies for its electricity generator business.
"The problem is coal is available more cheaply from nearby pits in the UK," he said. "It is hard to stack up the approach of shipping over coal from Peabody."
Sector watchers therefore say a split further down the line makes sense, freeing the most attractive partner Eastern for takeover suitors.
Eastern was taken over by Hanson last summer under a 2.5 billion pounds ($3.92 billion) agreed bid and is one of the best in the sector.

Looking at the characteristics of each business, Eastern is therefore seen as desirable to potential bidders, both in Britain and the United States for a number of reasons. "First it is set to become a major (electricity) generator in future, second it will take a lead in competing against British Gas in the gas market," Hawkins said.
UBS agreed that Eastern will use its three million customer base in electricity eventually to try to sell gas to the consumer gas market when it opens in 1998.

The internal valuation is helped to some extent by takeover hopes. But UBS's conglomerates analyst, Mark Cusack, warned the sector's bid premium has eroded and that electricity regulatory uncertainty could be a bit of a dampner on Eastern.

The main downside of Peabody Coal is its recent 600 million pounds asset writedown to 1.5 billion pounds, accounting for by U.S. federal levies for Black Lung (a compensation fund for industry-related illness) and Abandoned Land Mines funds.
Zafar Khan, analyst at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull, said this industry-wide levy posed an open-ended threat.
Hanson said its new accounting for the levies will also reduce the company's profits by around 70 million pounds.
Peabody's coal reserves consist of high sulphur coal in the U.S. East, used for power stations and steel production.
It also has low sulphur coal in the West. But UBS said that from January 2000, when new U.S. emission limits kick in, the demand for low sulphur coal will be greater.
"Peabody will well placed to exploit this trend," said UBS. ($1=.6385 Pound)
